title: The way returns
hookLine: returning is the movement of the Tao; yielding is its way (Tao Te Ching 40)

lines: A SWING GOES OUT AND COMES BACK.
cards: A swing goes forward as far as it can, hangs at the top for half a second, and comes back. Nobody calls that a failure. The coming back is how it gets to go forward again.
A tide runs out across the sand and returns. A breath goes out, and the next one comes in.
Chapter forty of the Tao Te Ching is short, and it opens on exactly this motion: the way things go out, and the way they come home.

teach.b: First, the line. James Legge set the opening as a little verse: "The movement of the Tao By contraries proceeds; And weakness marks the course Of Tao's mighty deeds."
Legge heard contraries: things turning toward their opposites. Other translators render the same opening as returning: the way moves by coming back. Some readers hear both at once.
What grows full turns toward empty; what goes out comes home. Second, where it returns to.
Chapter sixteen spoke of all things returning to their root, and chapter forty ends on the same note: everything under heaven comes from being, and being comes from non-being.
So the return isn't only a swing back and forth. It's a coming home to where things started.
Third, the other half: weakness marks the course. The way doesn't shove. It yields, the way water gives ground and still finds its level.
Returning and yielding sit side by side, like one motion seen from two angles. Fourth, closer to home. A lot of life is arranged around going out: further, faster, more.
Chapter forty quietly suggests that turning back is part of the movement, not a break in it. Coming back to a friend you drifted from. Picking up a book you set down halfway.
Returning to a practice after weeks away.
In this reading, returning isn't starting over.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter forty as a picture of the way moving in cycles, and some treat a return to an abandoned practice or relationship as part of that movement rather than a failure.

a warning that every road leads you backward
the Tao's motion of coming back, and of yielding

games.q: you drifted from a friend months ago, and they come to mind today. what does chapter forty's picture suggest?
o: wait until you have a good excuse for the gap.
turn back toward them, gap and all.
keep moving forward; going back is going backward.
games.why: the chapter treats returning as the way's own movement. coming back isn't the opposite of going forward.

practice: Let one thing come to mind that you once did and then set down: a walk you used to take, a person you meant to write to, an instrument in a closet, a prayer if you pray, or a quiet morning hour if you don't.
Don't scold yourself for the gap; just turn toward it, the way a breath turns and comes back in. Let your breathing do the teaching: out, a pause, and back.
